title: Effect of superconducting fluctuations on nonreciprocal dichroism and gyrotropy
abstract: We study the spatially dispersive conductivity of a two-dimensional noncentrosymmetric superconductor, demonstrating that it acquires a nonreciprocal, odd-in-wavevector component from fluctuation-induced Cooper pairs above the critical temperature $T_c$. Utilizing time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory generalized to include particle-hole asymmetry and the cubic Lifshitz invariant of trigonal superconductors, we compute the Aslamazov-Larkin contribution to the gyrotropic conductivity in closed form, including its complete frequency dependence. The dissipative part describes nonreciprocal directional dichroism: it is odd in frequency and displays a nonmonotonic dependence, peaking at frequencies comparable to the decay rate of fluctuating Cooper pairs. Its Kramers-Kronig dual component describes gyrotropic birefringence, which remains finite in the static limit and is strongly enhanced as the temperature approaches $T_c$. Both effects require simultaneously broken inversion and time-reversal symmetries, are dependent on particle-hole asymmetry in close analogy to the fluctuation Hall effect, and trace to the same asymmetric Cooper-pair dispersion responsible for the superconducting diode effect and the giant magnetochiral anisotropy observed near $T_c$. This critical enhancement dominates over the smooth normal-state gyrotropy, which we evaluate for the same band model as a baseline. Finally, we frame our analysis within the context of gated transition metal dichalcogenides like MoS$_2$, discussing the implications for probing superconducting dynamics through nitrogen-vacancy-center quantum noise spectroscopy.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes how fluctuations above the critical temperature ($T_c$) induce nonreciprocal electrical responses like dichroism and gyrotropy in 2D noncentrosymmetric superconductors. Using generalized Ginzburg-Landau theory, the authors show these effects critically depend on particle-hole asymmetry and require broken inversion/time-reversal symmetry. The results offer a pathway to probe superconducting dynamics using techniques like quantum noise spectroscopy.
main_problem: The study investigates how superconducting fluctuations induce nonreciprocal dichroism and gyrotropy in two-dimensional, noncentrosymmetric superconductors.
main_result: These nonreciprocal effects require the simultaneous breaking of inversion and time-reversal symmetries and are dependent on particle-hole asymmetry. The reactive component (birefringence) shows a critical enhancement as temperature approaches $T_c$.
method: The authors utilize time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory, calculating the Aslamazov-Larkin contribution to the gyrotropic conductivity in closed form.
model_or_system: The model is a two-dimensional noncentrosymmetric superconductor, exemplified by gated transition metal dichalcogenides like $	ext{MoS}_2$. The theory incorporates particle-hole asymmetry and the cubic Lifshitz invariant of trigonal superconductors.
key_observables: Nonreciprocal conductivity (dichroism and gyrotropy), which are analyzed via even-in-$k$ ($\sigma_{	ext{even}}$) and odd-in-$k$ ($\sigma_{	ext{odd}}$) components.
important_parameters: Temperature relative to $T_c$, particle-hole asymmetry parameter ($\gamma_2$), and the frequency $\omega$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that nonreciprocal terms do not alter the leading order results for gyrotropy near $T_c$ (Appendix B).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the frequency dependence of the derived fluctuation conductivity, showing distinct behaviors for the dissipative dichroism ($W(\varpi)$) and reactive birefringence ($V(\varpi)$).
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the theoretical framework using TDGL theory, then calculating the $	ext{AL}$ contribution to gyrotropy, analyzing the symmetry dependence on particle-hole asymmetry ($\gamma_2$), and finally discussing experimental implications for probing superconducting dynamics.
why_interesting: The explicit derivation of nonreciprocal responses from fluctuation effects provides a concrete theoretical link between broken symmetries (inversion/time-reversal) and measurable optical properties in superconductors, relevant to understanding exotic quantum states.
